doi:10.1002/jcal.70366.lead: While writing reports with AI, 21 students sometimes rejected suggestions after a disagreement. A rejection alone could mean the student had found a problem or was frustrated with the task.

doi:10.1002/jcal.70367.lead: The authors ask how students’ knowledge of AI relates to writing a research abstract with it. They distinguish knowing how the tool works from knowing how to use it and judge what it produces.

doi:10.1007/s00146-025-02400-z.lead: This paper asks how platforms make money by shaping what people notice. The authors argue that the design of a person’s digital surroundings matters for understanding how everyday habits develop.

doi:10.1007/s00146-025-02405-8.lead: This manifesto asks designers to consider what their tools help people pay attention to. The authors draw on Buddhist philosophy to make a case for technology that helps people notice and respond to others’ suffering.

doi:10.1007/s10648-026-10224-6.lead: The authors propose a way to decide which parts of a science or math task students should do themselves. They suggest starting with the skill being taught and checking whether students can reconstruct the essential steps.

doi:10.1007/s11423-026-10749-1.detail: Thirty business students practiced with the chatbot. Its final case appeared 146 times and drew 91 answers. A student could open the tutor more than once.
doi:10.1007/s11423-026-10749-1.lead: Students opened a GPT practice exam 224 times. Only 118 of those sessions included an answer to the first question.
doi:10.1007/s11423-026-10749-1.limit: The class used Moodle for a different topic. Its logs counted attempts without showing which questions students answered, so the totals cannot tell us which tool taught more.

doi:10.1007/s42438-026-00721-w.lead: In a proposed biochemistry lesson, students inspect an AI-generated experiment and explain how they would check it. Spotting a missing control gives the teacher something to discuss with the student.

doi:10.1007/s44163-026-02808-6.lead: Would you read a paper differently if its authors used AI to edit the grammar or to analyze the data? Matsui proposes showing readers different disclosures on the same paper to see what they check.

doi:10.1016/j.caeai.2023.100198.lead: In a research methods course in Ghana, students who used ChatGPT rated their critical, creative and reflective thinking higher after three weeks than classmates who used search tools. Those scores came from questionnaires.

doi:10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100571.lead: A review of 67 studies found that how teachers structured ChatGPT assignments mattered. The reviewers report that tasks with guidance for evaluating answers often supported both generating ideas and judging them.

doi:10.1016/j.chb.2024.108386.lead: Students researched sunscreen ingredients using ChatGPT or Google, then wrote recommendations from memory. The ChatGPT group described the task as easier but included fewer relevant points on average.

doi:10.1016/j.chb.2025.108779.lead: People used AI to answer 20 logic questions from a law school admissions test. In one study, they scored higher than a reference group yet estimated their own scores about four points too high on average.

doi:10.1016/j.chb.2026.109217.lead: Over five weeks, students played a business simulation. Researchers tracked who used its AI feedback and asked students how mentally demanding the game felt.

doi:10.1016/j.chbah.2026.100378.lead: Students worked in teams to solve a mystery with AI. Teams that spent more of their prompts creating ideas or checking their thinking did better on the task, even after researchers accounted for how many prompts they sent.

doi:10.1016/j.chbr.2026.101103.lead: Researchers asked people how they checked AI answers, then gave them a chatbot fact-checking task. People who scored higher on the questionnaire also judged the answers more accurately.

doi:10.1016/j.chbr.2026.101130.lead: Students used AI to build datasets about social networks. In higher-rated assignments, students more often told the tool both what to do and what background it needed.

doi:10.1016/j.chbr.2026.101340.lead: In take-home exams, students who described checking and revising AI suggestions tended to earn stronger marks. Some students who relied on generic AI answers missed what the course required in a definition.

doi:10.1016/j.chbr.2026.101420.lead: Researchers followed 668 medical students across eight months. Students answered questions about habits such as worrying and about their use of smartphone apps.

doi:10.1016/j.cognition.2026.106458.lead: In two experiments, people who had recently switched tasks lost less time on their next switch. When given a choice, they were also more likely to switch again.

doi:10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104977.lead: Students making slides used one AI tool to describe a picture and another to generate it. Researchers followed how the students judged and refined the images they put in their presentations.

doi:10.1016/j.compedu.2025.105448.lead: Researchers checked AI-generated study tips for a school reading and writing task. They compared automated checks with expert judgments and found that changing the order of two tips could change which one an AI judge preferred.

doi:10.1016/j.ijhcs.2025.103653.lead: A review of AI wellbeing apps asks what information a tool collects about you and how it decides when to step in. The authors use those questions to help designers weigh privacy and personal advice.

doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02590-6.lead: Judges correctly identified 67% of human-written photo captions as human and 46% of AI captions as AI. How well they told the two apart depended on the task.

doi:10.1038/s41598-025-01676-x.lead: Among 465 trainee teachers in Wuhan, those who reported using AI more also rated their progress toward teaching goals more highly. The survey asked trainees to judge that progress themselves.

doi:10.1038/s41598-026-70835-5.lead: After four weeks of exposure to AI-generated music, university students rated its usefulness and their trust in AI. Those who found the music more useful also reported greater trust.

doi:10.1038/s41598-026-77337-4.lead: Over twelve weeks, one animation class taught with AI tools made larger gains in the originality and detail of its ideas than a comparison class. The researchers scored a general thinking exercise rather than the animations students made.

doi:10.1038/s41598-026-78289-5.lead: At a university in Ghana, researchers surveyed 212 adult learners and interviewed six about how AI fit into their lives. Nearly all survey respondents had access to a smartphone, and fewer had access to a laptop.

doi:10.1038/s41598-026-78895-3.lead: Researchers followed 461 trainee teachers in China. Those who relied more heavily on AI tended to score lower on a measure of their willingness to think critically.

doi:10.1080/00131857.2026.2733624.lead: Drawing on experience teaching philosophy and ethics, the author argues for letting students question uncomfortable ideas and reason together. The essay also asks what happens when educators describe every challenge as a crisis.

doi:10.1080/02602938.2026.2731261.lead: The authors asked a chatbot a take-home exam question about whether machines think. In their example, getting beyond a polished list of ideas required someone to keep asking for explanations and guidance.

doi:10.1080/02602938.2026.2764204.lead: Kearney imagines grading four versions of the same assignment. Even a complete chat history might show a student accepting every suggestion without revealing whether they could explain the final answer.

doi:10.1080/09297049.2026.2744732.lead: Children and teenagers pressed a button in attention tasks. The timing of their responses varied more with higher ADHD symptom levels, and younger children with more symptoms also made more false alarms in one task.

doi:10.1080/10447318.2026.2722522.lead: A team reviewed 80 papers about how people think critically when using AI. They found that researchers often used the term without defining it, making it hard to tell whether studies measured the same skill.

doi:10.1080/10494820.2026.2732233.lead: At a Chinese university, English majors received writing feedback from AI or a teacher. Over the study, students in the AI group showed greater writing gains, especially in grammar.

doi:10.1080/10494820.2026.2744894.lead: Two groups took the same liberal arts course with the same teacher in different years. Students in the class that used ChatGPT rated their problem solving higher, and described setting limits on when to use it.

doi:10.1093/arclin/acag065.178.lead: In a clinic sample of 213 children and teenagers, performance on an attention test was linked to errors on another task that required stopping an automatic response or switching rules.

doi:10.1111/bjet.70094.lead: During a 25-minute classroom trial, students using two chatbots designed to guide their work reported more enjoyment and less boredom than students using standard ChatGPT. The groups showed no clear difference in immediate learning gains.

doi:10.1111/bjet.70100.detail: At one English college, students had 20 minutes for each set of unfamiliar math problems. They could work with a human tutor, an AI tutor or internet search.
doi:10.1111/bjet.70100.lead: On the first set of math problems, students with a human tutor started more questions than students with an AI tutor. The study counted attempts and left answer accuracy unmeasured.
doi:10.1111/bjet.70100.limit: One human tutor took part. The researchers counted which questions students started and asked how hard the work felt.

doi:10.1177/21582440261497404.lead: In a survey of 976 college students in China, those who trusted AI more also rated their own critical thinking higher. The scores came from students describing how they evaluate information.

doi:10.1186/s12888-026-08635-4.lead: Adults with insomnia said it was harder to switch their thinking and responded faster overall in a lab task. When the rule changed, the groups showed no clear difference in how much they slowed down or lost accuracy.

doi:10.1186/s40561-026-00477-7.lead: A review of 31 studies linked AI use with both a stronger desire to learn and greater dependence on the tool. The two patterns pointed in opposite directions for critical thinking.

doi:10.1186/s41239-024-00447-4.lead: Researchers built a version of ChatGPT that gives students hints and asks them to try an answer. It also keeps a log so students can revisit the questions they asked.

doi:10.1186/s41239-026-00632-7.lead: In a television production course, two groups of students followed a sequence of questions when they used AI. Both groups earned higher course grades than students who chose questions freely.

doi:10.1186/s41239-026-00644-3.lead: Of 93 studies in a review, only four documented both how students responded to AI suggestions and how they performed without AI. That leaves a gap between seeing who used the tool and knowing what they learned.

doi:10.1287/isre.2024.1282.lead: After Amazon introduced AI summaries of customer reviews, shoppers contributed more reviews. They wrote about features the summaries missed and added detail about ones already mentioned.

doi:10.1287/isre.2024.1431.lead: Real estate agents who saw how an AI priced apartments were less overconfident and handed more cases to it. Researchers saw no clear improvement in how accurately the agents priced apartments on their own.

doi:10.14742/ajet.11584.lead: In a 12-week study of 180 undergraduates, researchers compared teacher feedback with AI feedback designed to help students reflect. They reported gains in measures including time on task and school performance with the AI approach.

doi:10.1515/humaff-2026-0011.lead: The author proposes six steps by which getting useful help from AI might lead someone to hand over more of their thinking. The paper leaves open whether people actually follow that path over time.

doi:10.26300/80wn-ca81.lead: A Stanford team reviewed 52 studies of AI in education. Some found that students learned less when AI completed their work, while guided practice and tutoring showed more promise across studies, with mixed results.

doi:10.3389/feduc.2025.1697554.lead: The authors propose a tutor that plays the learner. A student explains an idea to the AI, and the AI can ask a follow-up question that invites the student to rethink the explanation.

doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1861548.lead: A survey of 848 learners found several ways of working with AI. Some described evaluating its answers closely, while others relied on them with little checking or remained skeptical and used AI very little.

doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1878665.lead: Across 26 studies of college students using AI, researchers found accounts of students checking sources after encountering convincing errors or invented citations. The review could not tell how often students checked.

doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1894455.lead: Future computing teachers at a university in Kazakhstan used ChatGPT on programming assignments. Although they said checking AI-generated code was important, their written accounts often gave few details about how they checked it.

doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1918374.lead: A review of higher education research found that AI sometimes helped students spot gaps and sometimes took over decisions about how to study. Much of the research came from settings with ample resources.

doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1929091.lead: Among 350 university students in Ghana, those who expected AI to be useful and easy to use were more likely to say they intended to use it. The survey asked about plans.

doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1944529.lead: The authors propose a way for writing teachers to combine demanding assignments with support for students using AI. They describe four combinations of expectations and support.

doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1949276.lead: Twenty students across four Latin American countries chose pictures to explain how they use AI at university. Some described it as a quiet companion and others described relief at getting help alongside unease about academic honesty.

doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1952725.lead: Undergraduates used AI to prepare short lessons and teach their classmates. In questionnaires afterward, students said AI made learning easier and more enjoyable.

doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1953305.lead: The author examines how international policy documents define cheating with AI and who they hold responsible when someone uses it in academic work.

doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1971754.lead: The authors propose a writing exercise in which students draw on more than one language, compare their wording with AI suggestions and explain what they choose.

doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1981900.lead: Walid Salameh reviewed 45 sources to ask what universities should teach when students can quickly find or generate an answer. The sources used different ways to assess thinking.

doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1983044.lead: Ten first-year students described creating AI images for a course assignment. They said choosing and judging the images helped them connect ideas from class. The study asked about their experience.

doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1997466.lead: The authors of this editorial ask how students could use AI to plan their work and interpret feedback while still deciding what to do next.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1261955.lead: Two university English classes in China took tests ten weeks apart. Scores rose in both classes, and the class using Duolingo gained more than the class using textbooks and teacher-led exercises.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2025.1598867.lead: Trainee teachers who compared recordings, used a chatbot and kept a journal reported larger gains in managing their singing practice. Both groups sang better after six weeks, with no clear difference in how much they improved.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2025.1666974.lead: What makes writing in a second language with AI feel demanding? Researchers developed an 18-question survey covering tasks such as giving instructions, checking suggestions and fitting them into a draft.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2025.1699320.lead: A chatbot can offer advice about stress, but keeping track of its advice can itself take effort. Ginto Chirayath and colleagues ask when that extra work helps people cope and when it becomes a burden.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1822091.lead: Among 878 university students in China, those who used AI more often also described depending on it more. Students who reported greater dependence gave themselves lower ratings for critical thinking.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1832219.lead: A review of research on teenagers’ phones found links between heavy use and modest attention and sleep difficulties. Studies of what happened when schools banned phones gave mixed results.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1870626.lead: Researchers surveyed Chinese university students three times over eight weeks. Students who reported greater reliance on AI at the start tended to report less confidence in their ability to learn four weeks later.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1873941.lead: In a lab study, 87 adults did short tasks with or without intermittent sounds and images. Researchers found no clear overall increase in errors when participants had to remember information or hold back an automatic response.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1878629.lead: People who said they handed the thinking over to AI also reported less interest in the work itself. Those who described using AI as a helper while making their own decisions reported more interest.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1884676.lead: Researchers tested a questionnaire that asks Chinese college students which parts of learning they hand to AI. A second group of 1,123 students helped check how the questions worked together.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1906199.lead: Across six writing classes, students with open access to AI produced the strongest assisted drafts. Students who had limits on AI help and reflected on their decisions later wrote the strongest essays on their own.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1913577.lead: Students at six Chinese universities rated the gap between what they could finish with AI and what they thought they could do alone. These were students’ own judgments.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1915597.lead: The authors suggest a test for chatbot support in later life. If someone practices a way to cope with a difficult situation during a chat, can they use it on their own later?

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1920791.lead: Forty students watched a short video about how wooden joints fit together. Adding motion to the AI-generated images made no clear difference to scores on a ten-question test.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1920947.lead: The researchers studied how doctoral students in China checked AI-assisted work that they would have to defend themselves. They traced the steps between asking for help with a research task and taking responsibility for the finished argument.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1924393.lead: In one data science course, students who received structured AI feedback scored higher on a later thinking test than similar students who received instructor feedback. The classes also differed in how feedback was given.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1929666.lead: Researchers asked 1,760 people who work with specialized terms how they give instructions to AI and how demanding that work feels.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1930030.lead: Across two surveys of 799 teenagers, stress and time spent on social media stood out in predicting reported school difficulties. The surveys cannot tell whether either factor caused those difficulties.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1939286.lead: University students rated how they used AI feedback, reflected on their work and judged information. The link between handling feedback and reported critical thinking varied with how much students said they reflected.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1941348.lead: Foreign-language students who feared falling behind or felt emotionally attached to AI were more likely to say they depended on it too much. The study surveyed 249 students at one Chinese vocational college.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1948254.lead: In one classroom project, students given steps for using AI asked it to compare and critique ideas more often. They asked it to finish answers for them less often.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1955418.lead: In a survey at a Chinese university, students who felt more stressed by AI also reported more difficulty adjusting to academic demands and less involvement in learning. The survey could not tell which came first.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1962253.lead: Some students who used a chatbot in an English writing class said it made asking for help less stressful. The study measured worry about writing and did not score the writing itself.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1971672.lead: Researchers at six Chinese vocational colleges compared students’ ratings of their AI skills, mental workload and ability to solve difficult problems. Students rated their own problem-solving skills.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1974520.lead: A review of AI in language learning looks at what students do after a tool gives feedback. The authors trace how trust enters decisions to accept a suggestion, check it, change it or reject it.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1975833.lead: Across four experiments, researchers studied how much people planned, checked their progress and reflected while working with AI. The experiments followed those habits during the task.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1978175.lead: Students in computing courses who rated their AI tools as more capable also described less unnecessary mental effort and greater confidence in their own abilities. The survey captured these views at one point in time.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1981428.lead: Engineering students judged two pieces of flawed AI advice. Those who did better on an AI knowledge test said they checked answers more often, and those reporting more checks gave better engineering answers.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1989652.lead: The authors propose that clear rules and clear responsibilities can shape how teachers decide when to use AI. They lay out questions researchers could test.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1993658.lead: Chinese teenagers who said they depended more on AI also reported more trouble directing their attention and earned lower exam scores. The researchers could not tell which came first.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1997631.lead: Among 450 Chinese art students, those who trusted AI more were more likely to say they planned to use it. The survey measured intentions.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1998976.lead: In a survey of 600 undergraduates, students who said learning took more mental effort also reported handing more of the thinking to AI. The survey cannot establish which came first.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1999813.lead: In a survey of 807 university physical education teachers, those more open to using AI also reported feeling better at work. The survey captured both at one point in time.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.2003031.lead: University students who read smoother AI explanations expected to do better on a test. In that experiment, researchers found no clear difference between groups when students took the test on their own.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.2006519.lead: Some university writers described using AI for a quick polish. Others described weighing its suggestions before deciding what to change in their English writing.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.2007654.lead: Students whose groups could use AI during a discussion scored slightly higher on a short individual test immediately afterward. The researchers did not give a later test to see what students remembered.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.2011342.lead: Among 982 university students in China, those who described themselves as more dependent on AI also reported more trouble keeping up their study effort. Students rated their own learning.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.2011597.lead: Among 530 medical students surveyed in China, about a third fell into a group that relied on AI for thinking through tasks yet reported little trouble putting work off. Another group reported both dependence and procrastination.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.2013021.lead: Among 15-year-olds in four Chinese regions, science scores differed with the reason students gave for using AI. The study could not tell whether using it changed their scores.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.2015390.lead: Five trainee math teachers in China used AI to plan lessons. In four decisions across two teachers, they spotted something uncertain and asked the same AI to check its own answer.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.2017882.lead: Music students at four Chinese universities answered five surveys about AI-assisted classes. Those who grew more involved in class also tended to say they became more absorbed in what they were doing.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.2022639.lead: Researchers examined online discussions about grading in the age of AI, mostly from Reddit. Detecting AI use and supervising work in class featured prominently. The counts describe what people discussed.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.2024279.lead: Graduate students who felt overwhelmed by AI suggestions for English writing reported more mental fatigue two weeks later. Four weeks later, they expressed less interest in using AI again.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.2024870.lead: Researchers surveyed students at three Chinese universities twice, twelve weeks apart. Those who reported making greater use of AI writing feedback later rated themselves higher at managing their English writing.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.2041306.lead: A survey of 1,050 students asked what work they handed to AI. Students who found checking its answers burdensome also reported feeling less engaged in their studies.

doi:10.3390/educsci13090856.lead: The researchers interviewed ChatGPT about its place in higher education and analyzed its answers about issues such as academic honesty. The interview shows how the chatbot described these concerns.

doi:10.3390/educsci13100998.lead: Researchers examined a lesson plan produced by ChatGPT. It included a warm-up, practice activities and a final assessment, giving teachers a draft they could adapt for their own classes.

doi:10.3390/educsci14020120.lead: Researchers asked ChatGPT to help plan and explain programming lessons. It produced study schedules and examples, giving the authors a way to examine the advice a learner might receive.

doi:10.3390/educsci16081291.lead: Luke Rowe proposes that students first practice a skill on their own, then try it with limited AI help. Once students show what they can do, teachers could let them hand over selected tasks.

doi:10.3390/educsci16091470.lead: Seventeen medical educators in the Netherlands discussed where AI might help students and when it could take over too much of their thinking. The interviews capture teachers’ concerns about what students can do independently.

doi:10.3390/jintelligence14070116.lead: Some Chinese university students who described using AI in more involved ways also said they relied on it more. The survey asked students to judge their own thinking skills.

doi:10.3390/jintelligence14080175.lead: Young adults described how often they used several kinds of media at once, then took thinking tests. Researchers found little overall link, though heavier multitaskers did slightly worse on a word-association task.

doi:10.3390/jintelligence14080182.lead: Among 239 trainee teachers surveyed in eastern China, those who said they relied more on AI also worried more about whether their lesson designs were truly their own.

doi:10.3390/jintelligence14100254.lead: University teachers in China described how they used their subject knowledge to check AI answers and asked students to explain their choices. The interviews tell us how teachers described checking, rather than how often it happened.

doi:10.3390/jintelligence14110286.lead: Thirty-eight students writing in Russian used longer words and more words that linked ideas when they could use AI. The researchers found no clear difference in total word count.

doi:10.3390/jintelligence14110288.lead: A survey of 942 trainee teachers asked about skills such as judging the quality of AI answers. Those who rated their skills and resources higher also gave themselves higher marks for trying new ways to teach.

doi:10.48550/arxiv.2610.38910.lead: College students in the US and Türkiye described how they worked with AI and whether they questioned its answers. The survey linked reworking AI-assisted tasks with reporting that they checked the output.

doi:10.48550/arxiv.2610.38950.lead: Ninth graders in three German schools practiced math with a chatbot before solving problems without it. The researchers traced when students asked how to do a problem, but conflicting statistics leave the link with test scores uncertain.

doi:10.48550/arxiv.2610.38990.lead: Seven researchers tried an AI math partner while playing the role of students. They said it helped to have room to try their own ideas, and described how getting the answer too soon could spoil that exchange.

url:https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14833v1.lead: After chatting with an AI adviser, people sometimes changed an answer they had gotten right. Without feedback on earlier answers, a previously inaccurate adviser persuaded them on 48% of the final trials.

url:https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15732v1.lead: People choosing an adviser for imagined decisions were more willing to hear AI advice than to let AI act for them. They declined AI in 12% of choices about getting advice and 38% of choices about handing over the decision.

url:https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16667v1.lead: People deciding how much of a potential £97 prize to donate rated AI advice more trustworthy than human advice. Researchers found no clear difference in the sums pledged by people receiving AI advice, human advice or no advice.

url:https://developer.apple.com/document.lead: Apple lets developers change what an app shows when a Focus is on. The choices a person sees depend on which filters the app supports.

url:https://feedback.one-sec.app/en/help.lead: The one sec app can ask why you want to open another app. You make that choice at the moment you reach for it.

url:https://freedom.to/.lead: Freedom lets you choose sites or apps to block for a set time. A session can cover more than one device.

url:https://openalex.org/W7127755367.lead: A review of 73 studies compares what happens when universities restrict AI, allow it freely, or guide students in using it. The authors offer questions for testing how those policies relate to effort and confidence.

url:https://openalex.org/W7161620989.lead: Would employees check a chatbot’s answer less carefully if talking to it felt like talking to a colleague? The authors propose interviewing employees and managers to explore that question.

url:https://openalex.org/W7164777577.lead: Researchers tracked readers’ eye movements while they read under different conditions. Some readers could block digital distractions themselves, while others had the distractions blocked for them.

url:https://www.amny.com/politics/google.lead: New York City schools disabled two Google AI tools on student Chromebooks, yet students reportedly still saw AI summaries in Search. City Council members asked Google if schools could turn those off and keep Search.

url:https://www.android.com/productivity.lead: Android’s Focus Mode lets you pause selected apps. Its activity records show time spent on the phone and how many alerts arrived.

url:https://www.apa.org/pubs/reports/ai-.detail: The guide suggests giving beginners a first try at a task before they compare their work with an AI answer. It also asks managers to notice when checking spills into time outside work.
url:https://www.apa.org/pubs/reports/ai-.lead: The American Psychological Association asks employers to give people time to check AI-assisted decisions and opportunities to practice the skills that checking requires.
url:https://www.apa.org/pubs/reports/ai-.limit: These are suggestions for workplace design. The guide does not test how much time a particular team will need.

url:https://www.cpr.org/2026/11/18/stude.detail: One Denver professor moved writing into class so he could watch an argument take shape. That left less class time for teaching political science.
url:https://www.cpr.org/2026/11/18/stude.lead: One Colorado student asked AI to help revise an essay using a teacher’s feedback. Another used it to check mechanics while keeping the voice of a college essay.
url:https://www.cpr.org/2026/11/18/stude.limit: The reporting describes choices teachers and students made. It does not measure what students learned.

url:https://www.edsurge.com/news/ai-has-.lead: Seventh-grade teacher Court Shuller describes having students draft on paper and discuss ideas aloud. The account explains the classroom choice and what the teacher observed.

url:https://www.edweek.org/technology/ha.lead: Lauraine Langreo reports on guidance for matching AI use to a child’s age and the skill they are practicing. Getting another practice problem gives a child a different job from receiving the homework answer.

url:https://www.edweek.org/technology/is.lead: Sarah Schwartz asks researchers what schools can learn from studies of AI in classrooms. Getting a chatbot to explain a problem leaves a student with a different task from getting it to complete the assignment.

url:https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2026/1.lead: The Electronic Frontier Foundation argues that people whose posts are removed by an automated system should be able to appeal to a person. An appeal gives them a chance to explain context the system missed.

The Electronic Frontier Foundation explains what it says happens when people exclude messaging apps from Siri AI. For example, keeping Messages out also means giving up Siri’s ability to read and reply to messages.

url:https://www.techpolicy.press/how-ai-.lead: The author asks what happens when a school treats a system’s guess about a student’s attention or emotions as a basis for decisions. The article examines who gets to interpret those signals.

url:https://www.techpolicy.press/new-per.lead: Richard Reisman and Richard Whitt propose giving people an AI assistant that helps decide what appears in their feeds. They ask how recommendations would change if users controlled whom the assistant serves.

url:https://www.techpolicy.press/the-int.lead: When an AI tool acts for someone online, who gets to decide what it can do? This policy essay asks how people can direct those actions and who should answer for them.

url:https://www.techpolicy.press/when-an.lead: When an AI shopping assistant clicks to buy, how does the seller know what the buyer agreed to? Camillia Rida argues that sellers need to know which decisions the buyer authorized.

url:https://www.theguardian.com/commenti.lead: Robin Kirman argues that an AI tutor ready with an answer at any hour could leave teenagers less time to work through uncertainty and decide what they think.

url:https://www.theguardian.com/technolo.lead: A housing investigator describes searching through long AI-written complaints to find the original problem. Another letter writer argues that people who use AI to put a grievance into words still deserve a hearing.
